column4:
5 – Meaningful inclusion and belonging for students with disabilities. Every student should be assigned to an age-appropriate general education homeroom and considered a member of that classroom first. Special education services should go with the student whenever possible, rather than requiring students to belong to a separate EC classroom. Students with disabilities should learn, eat lunch, attend specials, participate in activities, and be part of the everyday life of their school alongside their peers. Inclusion is not simply being physically present in the same building. Every student should know: I belong here.

5 – Broader enrichment choices in elementary school. World language is valuable, but it should not be the only significant enrichment opportunity offered to every student. Students have different strengths and interests. CHCCS should explore offering meaningful choices such as world languages, instrumental music, visual and performing arts, and other enrichment beginning in elementary school. A child who wants to learn Spanish should have that opportunity; a child who wants to learn an instrument should have that opportunity too. Our schools should cultivate many kinds of talent rather than deciding that one enrichment pathway fits every child.
column5:
5 – Belonging. Every child should attend the school where they live and be a full member of that school community. Students should not be separated, relocated, or sent to another school because they have a disability or need additional support. The supports and services should go to the child — the child should not have to go somewhere else to receive them. Neighborhood schools should belong to all children in that neighborhood.

5 – Presumed competence and high expectations. Every student should be presumed capable of learning, communicating, contributing, and belonging. Disability should never determine, especially at a very young age, a child’s access to peers, curriculum, extracurricular activities, or future opportunities.

5 – Community over segregation. Schools should intentionally build communities where students learn with and from people who are different from them. Inclusion benefits everyone, not only students with disabilities.

column8:
My hope is that this process begins with a very simple premise: every child belongs.

Students should attend the schools in the communities where they live and be full members of those school communities. A disability or need for additional support should not mean that a child is assigned to a separate classroom, program, or school away from their neighborhood peers. Services and supports should follow students; students should not have to leave their communities to access services and supports.

Future planning should move CHCCS toward genuine inclusion. Every student should have a general education homeroom, meaningful access to the general curriculum, peers, specials, extracurricular activities, and the full life of their school, with individualized supports provided as needed.

I also hope we broaden what opportunity looks like for all students. World language is valuable, but it should not be the only enrichment pathway emphasized in elementary school. Children should have opportunities to explore music and instruments, visual and performing arts, languages, and other interests. Different children have different gifts.

Buildings, boundaries, staffing and programs will change over time. Belonging should not. When making these decisions, I hope CHCCS continually asks: Does this plan create schools where every child who lives in this community can learn, participate and belong?

Why are Orange County and CHCCS separate in the first place? What makes Chapel Hill fundamentally different from Durham or Wake County?

Our declining student enrollment is directly connected to affordability. The high local tax burden makes Chapel Hill increasingly difficult for young families to afford, while the surrounding parts of Orange County do not face the same constraints.

Rather than continuing to cut programs and staff, shouldn’t we be asking whether the structure itself makes sense? Eliminate the special school tax and merge CHCCS with Orange County Schools. And if we’re serious about finding efficiencies, eliminating a redundant superintendent position would be a reasonable place to start.

I know we are concerned about closing schools, loss of jobs and disrupting our communities.  But, we need to be careful about letting our fears move us away from keeping students at the center of our choices.  It is so tempting to back into our corners and defend our little piece of turf.  We all, naturally, want to preserve our programs and school cultures.  But I would ask all of us to resist the comfort of the status quo and step into the discomfort of change, because our students need it.  Now is the time for student-centered decisions.  I understand that all of our stakeholders have the very best of intentions, but that does not mean that they know what is best for all of our students’ learning outcomes, particularly our economically disadvantaged, our language learning students who do not benefit from dual language programs, and black and brown students.  All of our students need us to be their champions, not to keep them in class with their friends, but to improve their chances in this world by giving them more targeted education that will improve learning outcomes.  

If we can open our minds to new ideas, new practices, and new programs, this could be a real opportunity.  We should be thinking about how we can create better schools and programs based on current student data.   We have a chance, as Chapel Hill Carrboro City Schools, to say yes, we are in the dead last state in student spending, and in a district that is going to lose employees and close schools—and yet, we are going to use this moment to improve student outcomes by looking critically at our system and making student-centered decisions, based on the data we have.   

The data tells us that district-wide, we have a significant population of students for whom we want to provide intentional, targeted support in reading and math during the critically foundational K-2 years.  The data tells us that we need significant support for our K-2 multilingual learners who are left out of the dual language programs.  The data also tells us the areas in K-2 that we need to prioritize, such as phonics and numeracy, ML support, and speech services.  But we also know from community and demographic data that we need family and parent support and training in order to best serve our lowest performing early learners.  

A K-2 intervention program for gen ed students well below grade level could allow us to provide targeted instruction designed to increase the probability of our lowest performing students meeting grade level standards before going to 3rd grade.  A program specifically designed to focus on these particular students and families could be a complete game-changer for all of our schools, as these K-2 students move up through the grade levels.

A K-2 Intervention program is just one program that should be considered when we are deciding how to move forward in this process.  I implore all of us to be creative enough to see this for the opportunity that it is to truly think and act differently and center students in our decision making.  We could have STEAM schools and dual language schools and an Intervention school, and anything else we determine our students need.  We don’t have to fight to save what we can.  Instead, we can work together to build exactly what our students need.  By centering student learning above all else, we can meet this moment and possibly live up to the words that we say.

column8: My biggest recommendation is to over-communicate throughout this process. Redistricting is long, complicated, and likely to change direction as new information and tradeoffs emerge. Most people do not have time to follow every meeting or presentation, so make it easy for the community to understand where things stand, what has changed, what decisions are coming next, and how people can meaningfully participate. Communication should extend beyond families who currently have children enrolled in CHCCS. School assignments affect neighborhoods, housing decisions, home values, and the broader community. Everyone has a stake in getting this right. Even this survey, for example, does not really offer "community member" as an identity, the closest option is Orange County resident. That may be a small thing, but it suggests a process primarily designed around current school families and staff rather than the broader community. I would also encourage the district to actively learn from other districts that have recently gone through redistricting and share that learning publicly. What approaches are emerging as best practices? What has worked? What has created unintended consequences? What are the major tradeoffs between stability, proximity, diversity, capacity, and other goals? Finally, communication should include explaining not only why the district is pursuing a particular approach, but why it choosing NOT to pursue reasonable alternative. If an option was considered and rejected, tell the community what it was and why. Understanding the tradeoffs and the reasoning behind decisions will build far more trust than simply presenting a recommended outcome.

Challenge: 
The central challenge is addressing changing enrollment without repeatedly disrupting children’s education, friendships, and school communities.

This survey does not adequately address that issue. Its questions feel too vague to capture meaningful disagreement and seem designed to produce a predetermined range of responses. It should ask directly whether families support moving currently enrolled students to different schools because enrollment patterns have changed. My answer is absolutely not.

I support adjusting boundaries, but those changes should apply prospectively as children enter school or transition to the next school level. Current elementary students should be allowed to remain at their school through fifth grade.

Enrollment will continue to fluctuate. If reassigning established students becomes the standard response, families will face recurring uncertainty and disruption. The district needs a long-term approach that accounts for population changes while protecting continuity for children already enrolled.  5 stars.

column8:
1) As a parent of a current student, I urge the district to carefully consider the significant impact that changing schools can have on students. Many students have spent years building relationships with friends, teachers, and staff while becoming comfortable and familiar with their school environment. Moving an established student to a completely different school means asking them to leave behind those important connections and adapt to an unfamiliar setting with new classmates, teachers, and routines. This type of transition can have a substantial effect on a student's emotional well-being, sense of belonging, academic performance, and overall school experience. While I understand the need to address enrollment and capacity challenges, I encourage the district to prioritize the social and emotional impact these changes may have on students and families.

2) The district should strongly consider grandfathering current students and allowing families to choose whether to remain at their current school. Students who are already established should not be forced to leave the school community they have invested years in building. Applying redistricting changes only to incoming or rising families would achieve the district's long-term enrollment goals while minimizing the immediate impact on students currently enrolled. This solution balances operational needs with the best interests of students and families, giving parents the ability to determine what is most beneficial for their child's educational and emotional well-being.

3) Special consideration should also be given to students with IEPs. These students often rely on established routines, familiar environments, and strong relationships with their teachers and support staff. A school change can be especially difficult, requiring them to rebuild trust with new resource teachers and adapt to an entirely new support system. Grandfathering current students into their existing schools while applying redistricting changes to incoming and rising families would help preserve continuity for these students and reduce the risk of disrupting the progress they have worked hard to achieve.

4) As the district evaluates redistricting options, it should also focus on ensuring that all schools provide a comparable level of resources and opportunities for students. Families should have confidence that regardless of which school their child attends, they will have access to high-quality IEP services, after-school childcare programs, extracurricular activities, academic enrichment opportunities, and well-maintained facilities. When disparities exist between schools in these areas, redistricting can feel less like a change in boundaries and more like a loss of valuable resources and opportunities. Before implementing boundary changes, the district should work toward creating greater consistency and equity across schools so that all students receive similar levels of support and access to programs.

5) The district should also recognize that proximity to a school does not always mean that elementary-aged children can reasonably walk there. Many parents, including myself, have concerns about community safety (we continually read about public gun violence in our community), traffic conditions (poor / lack of traffic signals), and other factors that influence transportation decisions. As a result, even families who live within walking distance may choose to drive their children to school to ensure their safety. For this reason, redistricting decisions should consider not only geographic distance, but also the practical realities families face. Providing a grandfathering option for currently enrolled students would allow parents to continue arrangements that are working well for their family while enabling the district to implement boundary changes gradually for incoming and rising students.

column8: In the school closure discussions, I found that there was a difficult balance of watching the board try to come up with solutions publicly while also not being operational experts. From a process standpoint, the conversation was much more clear, transparent and informed when scenarios were presented. Many of these are important issues for CHCCS, but redistricting is not necessarily the mechanism for addressing them.  

Functional capacity and adequate reserve capacity - 5
Capacity should reflect how school space is actually used, including Pre-K, EC services, specialized programs, intervention, and student supports. The district should also preserve reasonable reserve capacity for enrollment changes, future programs, and unexpected needs rather than treating every unused seat as excess capacity.
column5:
Flexibility and long-term adaptability - 5
Planning should preserve capacity and flexibility to respond to changes in enrollment, student needs, and educational programs without requiring frequent disruptive changes to school assignments.

Equitable access to programs and supports - 5
Students should have equitable access to specialized programs, services, and educational opportunities regardless of their assigned school.

Alignment with CHCCS Strategic Plan 2027 core values - 5
Long-term facilities, capacity, and student assignment decisions should reflect CHCCS’s adopted core values of Engagement, Social Justice Action, Collective Efficacy, Wellness, and Joy, rather than operating as a separate planning exercise.

column4:
Students being moved more than once — 5
Elementary boundaries are being drawn now, but the district’s own enrollment forecast shows the decline moving up through the grades over the next decade. A child reassigned in 2027 could face another change when middle school configuration catches up. Nothing in this process addresses that.

Students already enrolled being made to change schools — 5
This isn’t addressed anywhere in Policy 4150, the timeline, or this survey. The district is going to face enormous challenges in the coming years. It should be careful about creating upheaval that isn’t absolutely necessary.

Siblings assigned to different schools — 5
If current students are allowed to stay, a younger sibling assigned by the new boundary may not be able to join them, especially at a school that is closed to transfers.

Travel time for young children in the rural parts of attendance zones — 5
Some McDougle neighborhoods are already 2.5 miles from the school. Reassignment would put several of them farther from any alternative, in some cases three to four times farther.

Neighborhoods split between two schools — 5
Policy 4150 calls neighborhood groups “building blocks.” That only works if they stay whole.

Loss of walk zones where they currently exist — 5
Some neighborhoods can walk or bike to school today. This should be preserved. 

On the item about student populations shifting while boundaries haven’t adjusted — I rated it low because it’s written as a statement rather than a topic, and there’s no way to register disagreement with the premise. Boundary adjustment where it’s warranted isn’t unimportant to me. The claim as written isn’t something I can rate.
column5:
Continuity for students already enrolled — 5
A child who started at a school should be able to finish there.

Minimizing the number of students moved — 5
Balancing percentages and moving the fewest children are not the same goal. Please aim for the second.

Honoring existing walk zones — 5
Again, surprised not to see these mentioned anywhere in the survey.

Keeping neighborhoods whole — 4
Do not split them to make the numbers work. 

Transparency about the numbers behind the decisions — 5
The community engagement session slides gave program capacity and utilization for each school, which helped. We need to see how many students live in each planning segment, and what each building’s assessed capacity is next to its program capacity. Without those numbers, all we can do in November is look at a map and guess.

Two notes on the values that were listed above. Several of them needed an explanation of what they refer to. “High quality school meal service” could mean food or it could mean meal times — at the community session on October 8, the planner explained it was about scheduling meal times in overcrowded schools. There is no way to get that from the wording. The same problem applies to several other items.

“Ensuring well-balanced student populations across all school sites” is the item that matters most here, and I can’t tell what it means. One reading is that every school is about equally full. The other is that every school has a similar mix of students. You can’t always do both. I  support both, but my answer shouldn’t be read as endorsing one over the other. I’d ask that this item not be reported as though respondents understood it the same way.

The district’s greatest long-term challenge is improving academic quality. Strong instruction, experienced teachers, and high expectations should be the foundation of its future planning.

* Improving academic achievement — Priority 5: Establish measurable goals for reading, writing, mathematics, and science, and hold district leadership accountable for student progress.
* Retaining experienced, effective teachers — Priority 5: Make teacher retention a central priority through competitive compensation, strong classroom support, and reduced administrative burdens.
* Maintaining rigorous courses and academic opportunities — Priority 5: Preserve strong programs and advanced coursework while providing effective support for students who need additional help. Every student should have opportunities to grow without lowering academic standards.
* Keeping planning focused on educational outcomes — Priority 5: Evaluate building plans, redistricting, and proposed program cuts primarily by their effects on teaching quality and student learning. Administrative initiatives should serve the district’s educational mission.
* Using resources responsibly — Priority 4: Prioritize classroom instruction and demonstrate how major expenditures and organizational changes will improve education. Support should reflect students’ actual learning needs, with high expectations for students of every background.

The Board of Education should make academic excellence its guiding priority. The district’s long-term strength depends on the quality of education it provides and families’ confidence in its schools.

column4:
Transportation efficiency and ride times — 5. Boundary decisions should be scored on bus ride time and route simplicity, not just building capacity. The August 2026 bus problems showed how thin the margin is. Families on the east side of the district (Raleigh Rd / NC 54 corridor, Meadowmont) already face long rides to Culbreth when Phillips is closer; any redrawing should reduce, not add to, cross-town routing.

Feeder pattern alignment across all three levels — 5. Elementary boundaries should be drawn with the existing middle and high school assignments in mind, so that neighborhoods are not split across feeder paths. Even though middle and high schools are out of scope now, elementary lines that ignore them will force a second, more painful redistricting later. Please publish the elementary-to-middle-to-high mapping alongside each draft scenario so families can see the full path.

Stability and advance notice for incoming families — 4. Families relocating into the district make housing decisions one to two years ahead based on published assignments. Any future boundary or program change should carry a minimum one-year notice and grandfathering for students already enrolled, including those enrolled before arrival.

Consistent gifted and advanced-math access across middle schools — 3. AIG identification, compacted math, and LEAP access should not depend on which middle school a student is assigned to. Transfer and international students with no NC test history need a clear, published placement process before the school year starts.

Teacher staffing resilience at smaller schools — 3. Recent reviews describe core classes going without a certified teacher for extended periods. Consolidation only helps if the savings go into staffing stability at the remaining schools, especially for math and science at the middle level.

Transparency on enrollment and capacity data by school — 2. Publish current enrollment, program capacity, and the Asian/Hispanic/economically disadvantaged mix for each middle and high school alongside the scenarios, so the equity and balance tradeoffs are visible rather than implied.
column5:
Proximity — 5. Students should attend the school closest to home wherever capacity allows. Distance is the most concrete cost a boundary imposes on a family: it drives ride time, parent involvement, after-school participation, and sleep. When two scenarios balance enrollment equally, the one with shorter average and maximum ride times should win.

Predictability — 5. Families should be able to look up an address and know, with confidence, where a child will attend from kindergarten through 12th grade. Boundaries should change rarely, with long notice, and with grandfathering. A district where assignments are unstable is one families stop trusting when they choose where to live.

Coherent feeder paths — 4. Neighborhoods should move together from elementary to middle to high school. Splitting a cohort at each transition weakens the peer continuity that makes transitions work, and it makes every future boundary change harder than it needs to be.

Evidence over anecdote — 4. Scenarios should be scored on published, comparable metrics (ride time, utilization, cohort continuity, cost) so the community can see why one option was chosen over another. The Glenwood process lost trust where decisions appeared to shift without a visible rationale.

Fiscal discipline — 3. Consolidation should produce measurable savings that are redirected to classroom staffing. The value of closing a building is only realized if the remaining schools are better resourced, and the plan should say where the money goes.

Equity measured by outcomes, not composition — 3. Balancing school demographics is a reasonable goal but not an end in itself. The test of any scenario should be whether it improves access to strong teaching, advanced coursework, and support services for the students who need them, not whether the percentages line up.

We are a family of five relocating to Chapel Hill in August 2027 with children entering 6th, 9th, and 11th grade. We bought our home on the basis of published school assignments, so predictability matters to us in a very direct way.

Two comments on process. First, the 2013 redistricting left the district with middle school zones that cut across high school zones (Culbreth feeding both Carrboro High and East, for example). That is not a problem to solve in this elementary-only round, but it is a reason to draw elementary boundaries now with the full K-12 path in view, so the next process does not have to undo this one. Please show the full feeder path for each draft scenario.

Second, the published schedule and defined scope for this round are the right approach. Hold to both, and when a scenario is set aside, explain why in terms of the published criteria so families can follow the reasoning rather than guess at it.

One question: for families enrolling before the 2027-28 boundaries take effect, will the enrollment date or the effective date govern their assignment, and will students enrolled early be treated as continuing students for any future grandfathering? A clear answer would help every incoming family plan.

column8:
Rashkis is a warm and welcoming school.

Advocating for our students does not make us unwelcoming of others. It never has. We have said repeatedly and clearly that we welcome all students and families. What we have asked for is a plan that protects the children already in our care. Characterizing that advocacy as unwelcoming sets a dangerous precedent for every educator in this district who might one day need to speak up for a vulnerable child. And, as some of our staff will be displaced next year, it sends the message that fighting for students can be used against you. That is not a message this district nor our school board members should want to send.

As this district plans for future school assignments, I ask that every decision be evaluated first through the lens of our most vulnerable students, those who qualify for free and reduced lunch, those with IEPs, those whose families navigate this system in languages that are not their first. These students have the least power in any planning process and historically bear the greatest cost of decisions made without them in mind.

Stability matters for these children in ways that are not always visible on a spreadsheet. Relationships built over years between students, families, and staff cannot be reassigned. I ask that this district’s historical planning processes be examined honestly for whose interests they have consistently served, and that future planning make a different choice.

Every child deserves the best possible education, but its important to also remember that being fair doesn't mean being equal. Equality is not the same as equity. For example, it's not practical for every school to necessarily have all the specialty needs programs, it may be better to group some individuals with certain specialty needs and provide transportation for those few persons rather than recreate entire programs at each institution for small numbers of persons per institution. Sometimes it's better to coordinate transportation between schools for some groups of persons for partial day or partial week specialized needs. -5

In addition to minimizing distance students travel from home to school, maintain walk zones. This was a stated priority in the 2013 redistricting process. This allows for more buses to be utilized to transport those who live further away thus reducing distance and time required for bus routes, reduces use of non-renewable energy districtwide, reduces costs, and maintains higher property tax revenue for the district as real estate prices are partially correlated to distance from the districted school. -5

Encouraging well-balanced student populations across all school sites for the purpose of creating a diverse student population that engenders openness and trust to all persons. Note: The district cannot control changing population demographics. It's good to respond to changing needs, but the district cannot be expected to make certain that demographics are well-balanced across all sites. -5

I found this survey to be very confusing.  The email links reference "redistricting" but then the survey refers to "future planning".  I'm not sure if the context is more narrow (redistricting) or broad (future planning).  Overall I understand that the items listed are competing challenges and values, many of which I'm not significantly informed on the details or interdependencies.  As such, I'm concerned that the survey ranking results may not offer the insight desired.  

I have one key piece of feedback for the redistricting process, which I've included here:
We moved into the school district this calendar year.  Overall I have been very impressed;  I think the district is meeting or exceeding many expectations of a public school district.  The one glaring issue has been inability to provide adequate bus transportation for students.  I would consider it very unwise to take children in a walk zone and convert them to bus riders.  Not only would it be fiscally irresponsible, but it would add to a workload that is already not managed effectively.  Retaining proximity/walk zones is my biggest concern in the redistricting process.

My primary concern as CHCCS considers elementary redistricting is continuity and stability for students who are already established in their current school communities.

I previously shared this concern with the Board when Estes Hills Elementary was being considered for possible closure. I am a widowed parent, and my daughter has experienced the loss of her father. Her school community has become an important source of consistency, security, friendships, and belonging in her life.

I understand that CHCCS must consider enrollment, capacity, transportation, demographics, and the needs of the district as a whole when establishing future attendance boundaries. I am not asking the district to avoid necessary boundary changes. However, I strongly encourage CHCCS to distinguish between determining appropriate boundaries for future students and unnecessarily disrupting children who are already established in their schools.

As the district develops its redistricting proposals, I hope it will prioritize a grandfathering or continuity option for currently enrolled students, particularly when a student has already spent multiple years at the school and has significant individual or family circumstances for which maintaining an established school community is especially important.

If transportation is a concern, I would also encourage the district to consider allowing families who are able and willing to provide their own transportation to remain at their existing school through the end of elementary school.

For my daughter, remaining connected to the school community in which she has already built relationships and stability is extremely important. This is the same concern I raised during the school-closure discussion, and I hope continuity for existing students will be considered before redistricting scenarios and transition policies are finalized, rather than only after families are affected.

During the early years of a child’s academic journey (Pre-K, kindergarten, and first grade), we should place greater emphasis on teaching the behavioral, emotional, and practical life skills they need to thrive. Children should learn how to brush their teeth, wash their hands, tie their shoes, manage conflicts, regulate their emotions, and behave appropriately in a classroom before we place the primary emphasis on academic skills such as reading and writing.

Many children are entering school without these essential life skills, yet there is no formal, dedicated time in the curriculum to teach them. Instead, the responsibility falls on individual teachers to decide whether these skills need to be addressed and to find time to teach them while keeping up with an already demanding academic curriculum. We need to recognize these foundational skills as an essential part of early childhood education and provide dedicated time and structured instruction to ensure that all children have the opportunity to develop them.
